div.head: IV Atr 4.1
div.ab: Si pugnet, antequam sibi rectum postulet, ac uiuat, emendet regis burhbrece quinque libris.
Si pugnet antequam sibi rectum postulet ac vivat, emendet regis burhbrece quinque libris.
Wenn er [in Rache] ficht, bevor er sich [friedlich] Recht fordert, und [dabei] leben bleibt, büsse er die Verletzung [des Sonderfriedens] einer königlichen Stadt mit 5 Pfund [dem König].

If he fights [in vengeance] before he demands his right [peacefully], and [in doing so] stays alive, let him pay compensation for breach of [the special peace of] a royal borough with 5 pounds [to the king].
If, before demanding justice, he has recourse to violence, but does not lose his life thereby, he shall pay 5 pounds for breach of the king's peace.

note.seg: Original hatte gif he feohte, ærþamþe he him rihtes bidde laut Af 42. II As 3. Vgl. Gl Selbsthilfe 2; Blutrache 14d
The original had gif he feohte, ærþamþe he him rihtes bidde, to judge by Af 42. II As 3. Cf. Gl Selbsthilfe 2; Blutrache 14d

Q und alle Erklärer verstehen den Angreifer, also in Ggs. zu iaceat 4. Mir scheint jedoch, das Original meinte Subjektswechsel: ‘wenn Angegriffener nicht erschlagen wird’, bei Halbverletzung (s. d. 1ff.), kommt Missetäter mit Geldbusse davon

Q and all commentators take this to mean the attacker, i.e. in contrast to iaceat 4. It seems to me, however, that the original intended a change of subject: ‘if the man attacked is not slain’, in a case of half-breach (see that word 1ff.), the wrongdoer gets off with a money compensation

Q versteht burgbryce zwar als Verletzung der Stadt (s. d. 11—f); und dies beweist, dass einem Juristen um 1114 eine besondere Strafsumme hierfür möglich schien. Allein dass sie je wirklich war, zeigt es nicht und scheint sonst nicht belegbar. Freilich geschieht auch diese Missetat in der Stadt. Der besondere Stadtfrieden aber findet seine Busse in 4, 2 mit nur 30 Schilling. Steenstrup (Danelag 359) nimmt daher regis burgbryce im Sinne: ‘Einbruch ins königliche Haus’, den er zuletzt bei Af 40 findet. [Im Domesday ist dieser Wortsinn erhalten: Qui per noctem effringebat civitatem (d. i. burg brece), c sol. (= 5 ℔) emendabat regi, non vicecomiti; Berkshire I 56b.] Mir scheint in diesem Zusammenhange diese Bed. ganz unmöglich, auch kostet cyninges burgbryce dort nur 120 Schilling = 2½ ℔. Schmids Besserung zu borgbryce trifft m. E. den Sinn des Originals: Blutrache vór Aufforderung zum Rechtsgang kostet das ‘Königsschutz’ (s. d. Gl 1. 5. 8) heissende Strafgeld von 5 ℔. Jener selbige Lateiner schrieb burgbrece statt borgb. auch Hn 12, 2. 35, 2

Q does indeed understand burgbryce as breach of the town (see that word 11—f); and this proves that to a jurist c. 1114 a special penal sum for this seemed possible. But it does not show that one ever really existed, and this seems not to be attested elsewhere. Admittedly this offence too takes place in the town. But the special peace of the town receives its compensation in 4, 2, at only 30 shillings. Steenstrup (Danelag 359) therefore takes regis burgbryce in the sense ‘breaking into the king's house’, which he finds last in Af 40. [This sense of the word survives in Domesday: Qui per noctem effringebat civitatem (i.e. burg brece), c sol. (= 5 ℔) emendabat regi, non vicecomiti; Berkshire I 56b.] In this context this meaning seems to me quite impossible; moreover, cyninges burgbryce there costs only 120 shillings = 2½ ℔. Schmid's emendation to borgbryce catches, in my opinion, the sense of the original: blood-feud before a demand for legal process costs the fine of 5 ℔ called ‘king's protection’ (see that word in Gl 1. 5. 8). That same Latin writer also wrote burgbrece instead of borgb. in Hn 12, 2. 35, 2

Dieselbe Summe schon 3, 2². Maitland Domesday 184 meint mit Unrecht, Ælfreds 120 Schilling für burgbryce, was er für richtig hält, sei irrig durch Q als 100 verstanden und Normannisch als 5 ℔ ausgedrückt worden

The same sum already at 3, 2². Maitland Domesday 184 wrongly thinks that Ælfred's 120 shillings for burgbryce, which he holds to be correct, were misunderstood by Q as 100 and expressed in Norman terms as 5 ℔
Liebermann suggests that, in the original text, these words probably referred to the person attacked and have been misunderstood by the translator.

burhbrece here can hardly be anything but a corruption of borgbryce (cf. Af. 3), as suggested by Schmid and Liebermann. Liebermann points out that the same translator wrote burgbrece instead of borgbrece also in Hn. 12, 2; 35, 2.
